extracted.intended_audience: marine biologists, zoologists, and fisheries researchers conducting benthic (sea-bottom) surveys
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological guidance for sampling, mapping, and quantifying sea-bottom (benthic) animal communities, with practical recommendations on equipment, sampling design, and interpretation for fishery and ecological studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer quantitative bottom-sampler over dredge for representative illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the bottom-sampler is able to give a true and quantitative representative illustration of the bottom fauna.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bottom-sampler yields animals per unit area (per sq. metre) and so allows quantitative measurement of community content; by contrast, the dredge tends to take animals 'on, not in, the bottom' and mixes epi-fauna from different communities, and 'a true illustration of the fauna on the sea bottom it never has given and never will give.' Use the bottom-sampler when quantitative, per-area data are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map level sea-bottom communities using frequent-occurrence organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: By means of the bottom-sampler we may... using the most frequently occurring organisms, easily map out the communities of the level sea-bottom, and determine its content of fish-food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify characteristic (most frequent) taxa in samples and use them as indicators to delineate community types (e.g., Venus mussel community, Amphiura filiformis community). Produce distribution maps of these communities to allow comparisons among areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design sampling with sufficient replication; use probability theory to assess accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of probability will indicate the degree of accuracy; many samples will give, as a rule, more and more exactitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sample sizes and numbers to achieve the desired precision; use many samples to reduce uncertainty and to estimate seasonal and interannual variability. Statistical/probabilistic methods should be used to infer accuracy from the number and distribution of samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare only like-for-like communities when assessing food amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: I realised that I should compare, first of all, the amount of food in places with the same kind of animal population, and I had to map out these places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because animal size/composition (e.g., small fast-growing vs. large carbonate-rich organisms) affects food value, avoid direct quantitative comparisons of places with different community composition without normalization or partitioning by community type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for and treat epi-fauna separately due to patchy distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The epi-fauna is, as a rule, scattered over the bottom in spots, and it is not always easy, in single cases, to say what is the reason for its existence; it is therefore not possible to give its distribution on a chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that organisms fixed to objects (stones, shells, wrecks) form patchy epi-faunas that cannot be reliably mapped by standard grid sampling. Distinguish epi-fauna from level-bottom communities in analysis; dredges will collect both and can confuse interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dredge for collecting rare species and specimens, not for quantitative estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: The dredge has given excellent information to zoologists wishing to collect rare animals for preservation... but a true illustration of the fauna on the sea bottom it never has given and never will give.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dredging when the objective is to obtain specimens (rare taxa, taxonomic work, oysters, etc.), but do not rely on dredge samples for estimates of abundance per unit area or for mapping community distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify fish-food and productivity per unit area and follow seasonal/yearly variations
rubrics_metrics.description: We may determine how the number of organisms varies at different seasons and in different years... If we examine what the fishes eat of these organisms we may determine whether they are good or bad areas for this or that species of fish, and may get a fair idea of the productivity of the sea-bottom as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated quantitative sampling to estimate biomass/abundance of food organisms, relate it to fish diets to assess habitat quality for target species, and infer productivity (annual production vs standing stocks) accounting for life-history differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan spatial coverage proportional to study goals; provide concrete sampling-intensity examples
rubrics_metrics.description: With a good steamer I could in one month map out the whole of the North Sea as to its animal communities, I would take between 500 and 1000 samples spread over the whole of the North Sea, out to the 100-fathom line, about one or two per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine number of stations and temporal effort based on area and desired resolution. Example: mapping the North Sea (to 100 fathoms) might require 500–1000 samples; choose sampler size and tow frequency to meet those targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose sampler size appropriate to objectives; recognize sampled-area implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a bottom-sampler of 0·2 sq. m I should then have taken up only the animals of an area at 100–200 sq. m., but I am sure that I should get all the species of the common uniformly-distributed animals of the whole area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sampler mouth area with awareness of the effective area sampled and its implications for detecting common vs rare species. Smaller samplers may be efficient at characterizing common, uniformly distributed taxa but will miss many rare organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize common, characteristic species for fisheries-relevant studies
rubrics_metrics.description: I should not catch many rare animals, but I do not care for rare animals; the main thing is to know the animals that make up the great bulk of the bottom population, to know their distribution and their weight per square mile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fishery productivity and management questions, focus sampling and analysis on species that constitute the bulk of biomass/food resources rather than on rare taxa, unless the study explicitly targets rarity or biodiversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider density-dependent (overcrowding) effects when linking food to fish growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference in growth-rate of the plaice... was found later on to depend not only upon the amount of food on the bottom, but also upon the different number of plaice living there on each square mile. The idea of overcrowding for sea-fishes was introduced for the first time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing fish growth or condition, account for both per-area food availability and fish population density; density can modulate per-capita food access and growth rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations of the bottom-sampler and adapt methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The bottom-sampler is not able to solve every question; it cannot, e.g., take animals living very deep in a hard bottom, and the apparatus must be modified for special work, according to the size of the ship used, the depth at which you are working, etc., and it is necessary to supplement the investigation by means of other apparatus, fishing-gear, dredges, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about questions the bottom-sampler cannot answer (deep-burrowing fauna in hard substrate, very rare taxa). Modify sampler design and supplement with other gear or methods depending on depth, substrate, vessel capability, and specific research aims.
